<reason>The debate turned on a single structural question: what does "standing commitment" actually bind that periodic renewal does not? CON identified this ambiguity early ([B2.1]-[B2.2]) and pressed it relentlessly through pressure questions, rebuttal 2, and closing, forcing a clean dilemma: either the commitment locks resources (undermining PRO's own concession that a Taiwan contingency might need the same interceptors) or it doesn't bind anything beyond rhetoric (collapsing into CON's proposed model). PRO's answer—distinguishing "default continuation" from "default expiration"—was a real and defensible institutional-design point, but PRO never fully developed it (e.g., via status-quo-bias or sunk-cost framing) and instead kept restating "continuing claim on resources" language that CON was able to reuse against PRO in the closing exchange ([B5.1]-[B5.2]). PRO had good uncontested ground on industrial planning incentives and the "insecure negotiation" argument, which CON never squarely engaged, but the debate's decisive axis was the bindingness dilemma, and CON controlled it more convincingly across rounds. CON's Taiwan opportunity-cost framing also gave concrete stakes that PRO's "sequencing and reserves" response only partially neutralized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B4.1]/[B5.1]-[B5.2] exchange, exploiting the tension between PRO's claim that "standing" creates a durable resource claim and PRO's simultaneous admission that individual transfers remain reallocable—an unresolved contradiction that PRO's closing restated rather than resolved.</best_rebuttal>
